DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review of the Thornbury Food Waste Feasibility Study

**Overall:** The pilot is a sound basis for planning, and most of the arithmetic is correct. But three of the author's central claims are contradicted by the study's own figures:
- that participation held up across houses and flats;
- that treatment is local;
- that the service is fully funded.

The flats finding changes how the service should be designed. Brookfield's capacity cap and an error in the participation rate together remove the funding margin. Cabinet should not approve the roll-out on this version of the study.

## What checks out

- **Participation rates in Table 1:** 2,112 / 3,200 = 66%, 168 / 800 = 21%, and 2,280 / 4,000 = 57%, all as stated.
- **Disposal saving per tonne:** £112 − £38 = £74, and 3,290 t × £74 ≈ £243,000.
- **Vehicle cost:** 6 × £165,000 = £990,000, which over 7 years is £141,400 a year.
- **Crew cost:** 6 crews × 2 operatives × £34,000 = £408,000.
- **Totals:** costs sum to £733,400, and £733,400 − £243,000 = £490,400.
- **Contamination:** under 2% is a genuinely good result, and the falling missed-collection reports are encouraging.

## Main problems

### 1. Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses, not "broadly similar"

The rates were 66% in houses and 21% in flats. Flats also produced less waste per participating household: 1.4 kg a week against 1.9 kg.

The conclusion in the study, the recommendation and the author's note all depend on the claim that the two housing types are similar, and the table shows the opposite. A uniform service is supported for houses. For flats, the pilot shows that the standard model does not work.

Flats are about 10,400 of the district's households. They need a separate approach, such as communal food bins or different container placement. Lower participation in flats is a common pattern, so the result is believable, not an anomaly.

### 2. The projection uses 64% participation, but the pilot measured 57%

No figure of 64% appears anywhere in the pilot data. The pilot's mix of housing (20% flats) is the same as the district's, so the pilot's overall 57% applies directly.

Recalculated by housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That is about 2,870 tonnes, against the 3,290 projected. A smaller point: the table's combined figure of 1.9 kg rounds up a true weighted figure of 1.86 kg.

The pilot also ran from launch, during January to June. Participation often dips once a service is no longer new, and food waste volumes vary by season. That means 2,870 tonnes is an estimate, not a conservative figure.

### 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029

Even on the corrected projection, about **1,070 tonnes a year** has no contracted treatment route. On the study's own figure of 3,290 tonnes, the gap is about 1,490 tonnes.

The excess would have to go to the next nearest plant, 46 miles away, or stay in the residual bin. The study gives:
- no gate fee for the second plant;
- no haulage cost for a round trip of about 92 miles;
- no collection time lost while vehicles travel there.

So the claim that "treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the tonnage. The £74-a-tonne saving can only be relied on for the 1,800 tonnes Brookfield will take.

### 4. "Fully funded" is not established

With the corrected tonnage, and assuming *every* tonne gets the full £74 saving with no extra haulage:
- Saving: 2,870 × £74 ≈ **£212,000**
- Net cost: £733,400 − £212,000 ≈ **£521,000**

That is already above the £520,000 allocation, before any of the following are added:
- **Overflow tonnage:** the gate fee and haulage for the roughly 1,070 tonnes above Brookfield's cap.
- **Crew on-costs:** if £34,000 is salary rather than total employment cost, employer National Insurance and pension add roughly 25–30%, about £100,000–£120,000.
- **Cover for absence:** six crews with no relief staff for leave or sickness.
- **Capital and financing:** £990,000 of vehicles must be paid for when ordered in December 2026. Depreciation spreads the cost but doesn't fund the purchase. The financing cost, or the capital source, needs stating.
- **Smaller costs:** supervision, the launch phone line and web page, and depot space.

The allocation is also **provisional**. The document says only that the Government "has indicated" funding will be provided, which is weaker than the author's "fully covered."

The realistic position is a **shortfall of tens of thousands to around £200,000 a year**, depending on the cost of the overflow tonnage and the crew on-costs. That should be quantified before Cabinet decides.

### 5. Check the statutory deadline

From memory, the Simpler Recycling rules required councils in England to start weekly household food waste collections by **31 March 2026**, with transitional arrangements for some councils. I haven't checked this against the regulations. If my memory is right, a start date of April 2027 needs either a transitional exemption or an explanation.

Section 1 states the requirement but not the deadline. It should cite the regulation and Thornbury's position under it.

## Smaller points

- **Satisfaction survey.** The 81% rating comes from "surveyed pilot households," with no sample size or response rate given. Households that took part are more likely to answer such a survey, so the figure probably overstates satisfaction among all households.
- **Liners.** Households would get a three-month supply at launch, but the annualised costs include liners. Is supply ongoing? If liners stop after three months, participation may drop, and the pilot can't show the effect because it supplied liners throughout.
- **Vehicle numbers.** Six vehicles were sized on the 64% figure. With corrected tonnage the round could be re-optimised, but the overflow trips may need some of that vehicle time back.

## What Cabinet would need before approving

1. Correct the projection to the pilot's measured participation, calculated separately for houses and flats.
2. Design and cost a separate collection model for flats, rather than assuming a uniform service.
3. Get a treatment route and price for the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800-tonne cap until 2029.
4. Restate costs with full employment on-costs, absence cover, vehicle financing and any overflow haulage, and compare the result with the allocation. State clearly that the allocation is provisional.
5. Confirm the statutory start date and Thornbury's position under it.

The vehicle-ordering deadline is real. One option is to authorise the vehicle order separately, if there is a basis for funding it, while the revised financial case is prepared. That avoids losing the April 2027 slot while the corrections above are made.
